text:
IN THE SUPREME COURT OF BRITISH COLUMBIA

Citation:

Nesbitt v. Neufeld,

2010 BCSC 1751

Date: 20101208

Docket:
S118846

Registry: New Westminster

Between:

Patrick Michael Nesbitt

Plaintiff

And

Wendy Lee Neufeld

Defendant

Before: The Honourable Madam Justice Gropper

Reasons for Judgment

Counsel for the Plaintiff:

Appearing
on his own behalf

Counsel for the Defendant:

M.A.
Misner

Place and Date of Hearing:

New
Westminster, B.C.

March
5 and November 12, 2010

Place and Date of Judgment:

New
Westminster, B.C.

December
8, 2010

[
1
]

The defendant, Ms. Neufeld, applies to strike
Dr. Nesbitt’s statement of claim. She also seeks an order that Dr. Nesbitt is
in breach of the order of Truscott J. of October 14, 2009.

Background

[
2
]

Dr. Nesbitt and Ms. Neufeld are the parents of a
child born in 2003. They were not married. Issues regarding custody and access
arose between them which are now before the Provincial Court under the
provisions of the
Family Relations Act
, R.S.B.C. 1996, c. 128.

[
3
]

On July 28, 2009, Dr. Nesbitt applied for
default judgment against the defendant. On August 28, 2009, Ms. Neufeld applied
to strike Dr. Nesbitt’s statement of claim.

[
4
]

On October 14, 2009, Truscott J. refused to
grant Dr. Nesbitt default judgment and ordered that he provide to Ms. Neufeld’s
counsel no later than October 28, 2009, unaltered copies of any exhibits to his
affidavit materials and that he not set his notice of motion until those
documents were provided.

[
5
]

The plaintiff’s application for default judgment
and defendant’s application of August 28, 2009, seeking to strike Dr. Nesbitt’s
statement of claim was heard by Madam Justice Hyslop on November 24, 2009. She
adjourned Dr. Nesbitt’s application for default judgment. She struck paragraphs
2-164 of the statement of claim. The plaintiff was allowed to amend his
statement of claim by December 18, 2009, provided that he deliver a copy
of the filed amended statement of claim to the defendant’s solicitor no later
12:00 p.m. on December 22, 2009. The defendant had liberty to reapply to have
the amended statement of claim reviewed by the court. In her reasons, Hyslop J.
granted special costs to the defendant:
2010 BCSC 42
.

[
6
]

The defendant, through her counsel, received an
unfiled, amended statement of claim by fax at 6:33 p.m. on December 21, 2009.

[
7
]

When this hearing commenced on March 5, 2010,
Dr. Nesbitt referred to his draft amended statement of claim. He did not advise
counsel or the court that he had actually filed a statement of claim on March
3, 2010. That fact was provided by counsel for the defendant on the second day
of the hearing, November 12, 2010, after he searched the court file.

[
8
]

Ms. Neufeld’s counterclaim was heard by Mr.
Justice Crawford under Rule 18A. In his decision:
2010 BCSC 1605
,
Crawford J. awarded special damages to Ms. Neufeld for defamation and
breach of privacy as well as special costs.

Application
to Strike

[
9
]

There are two issues: whether Dr. Nesbitt
complied with the order of Hyslop J. which required him to file and serve
his amended statement of claim on or before 12:00 p.m. December 22, 2009; if
Dr. Nesbitt is not in breach of that order, is his amended statement of claim
in conformance with
Rules of Court
?

[
10
]

I find that Dr. Nesbitt did not comply with the
order of Madam Justice Hyslop, particularly, that he deliver a copy of the
filed amended statement of claim to the defendant’s solicitor no later than
12:00 p.m. on December 22, 2009. Counsel for the defendant received an unfiled
copy of the amended statement of claim on December 21, 2009.

[
11
]

The order of Hyslop J. was explicit. A filed
amended statement of claim was to be served on the defendant’s solicitor on
December 22, 2009. Dr. Nesbitt did not do that. He filed his statement of claim
on March 3, 2010, several months later.

[
12
]

I have no hesitation in finding that Dr. Nesbitt
has breached the terms of the November 24, 2009 order of Hyslop J. While
my finding in regard to the above issue does not require me to consider whether
the amended statement of claim conforms with the
Rules of Court
, I will
go on to address that matter. The positions of the parties and the legal principles
which were presented to me are identical to those which were presented to
Hyslop J. For ease of reference, I will reproduce paras. 8 through 21
of her decision:

POSITIONS

Ms. Neufeld

[8]        Ms. Neufeld alleges that Dr.
Nesbitt’s statement of claim discloses no reasonable claim (Rule 19(24)(a) of
the Rules), the pleadings have structural defects (Rule 19(24)(b) and (c) of
the Rules) and is an abuse of process (Rule 19(24)(d) of the Rules).

[9]        Further, the statement of claim
is prolix and refers to evidence offending Rule 19(1). In addition, the
statement of claim includes conclusion of law without pleading the material
facts on which it relies.

[10]      Ms. Neufeld argues that the
statement of claim fails to establish a nexus between the alleged wrongs and
quantifiable damages to Dr. Nesbitt.

[11]      Ms. Neufeld alleges all of this
makes it impossible for her to understand the case she must meet.

Dr. Nesbitt

[12]      Dr. Nesbitt’s position is that he
has followed the Rules and followed the instructions of self-help resources in
drafting his statement of claim.

THE LAW

[13]       Rule 19 of the
Rules
are
as follows:

Contents

(1) A pleading
shall be as brief as the nature of the case will permit and must contain a
statement in summary form of the material facts on which the party relies, but
not the evidence by which the facts are to be proved.

…

Pleading
conclusions of law

(9.1)
Conclusions of law may be pleaded only if the material facts supporting them
are pleaded.

…

Where
particulars necessary

(11)  Where the
party pleading relies on misrepresentation, fraud, breach of trust, wilful
default or undue influence, or where particulars may be necessary, full
particulars, with dates and items if applicable, shall be stated in the
pleading. If the particulars of debt, expenses or damages are lengthy, the
party may refer to this fact and instead of pleading the particulars shall
deliver the particulars in a separate document either before or with the
pleading.

Particulars in
libel or slander

(12)  In an
action for libel or slander,

(a) where the
plaintiff alleges that the words or matter complained of were used in a
derogatory sense other than their ordinary meaning, the plaintiff shall give
particulars of the facts and matters on which the plaintiff relies in support
of that sense, and

(b) where the
defendant alleges that, in so far as the words complained of consist of
statements of fact, they are true in substance and in fact, and that in so far
as they consist of expressions of opinion, they are fair comment on a matter of
public interest, the defendant shall give particulars stating which of the
words complained of the defendant alleges are statements of fact and of the
facts and matters relied on in support of the allegation that the words are
true.

…

Scandalous,
frivolous or vexatious matters

(24)  At any
stage of a proceeding the court may order to be struck out or amended the whole
or any part of an endorsement, pleading, petition or other document on the
ground that

(a) it discloses
no reasonable claim or defence as the case may be,

(b) it is
unnecessary, scandalous, frivolous or vexatious,

(c) it may
prejudice, embarrass or delay the fair trial or hearing or the proceeding, or

(d) it is
otherwise an abuse of the process of the court,

and the court may
grant judgment or order the proceeding to be stayed or dismissed and may order
the costs of the application to be paid as special costs.

[14]      Section 3(2) of the
Limitation
Act
reads as follows:

Limitation
periods

...

(2) After the
expiration of 2 years after the date on which the right to do so arose a person
may not bring any of the following actions:

(a) subject to
subsection (4) (k), for damages in respect of injury to person or property,
including economic loss arising from the injury, whether based on contract,
tort or statutory duty;

(b) for trespass
to property not included in paragraph (a);

(c) for
defamation;

(d) for false
imprisonment;

(e) for
malicious prosecution;

(f) for tort
under the Privacy Act;

(g) under the
Family Compensation Act;

(h) for
seduction;

(i) under
section 27 of the Engineers and Geoscientists Act.

[15]      The British Columbia Court of
Appeal in
Young v. Borzoni
,
2007 BCCA 16
, at para.
19
, stated the
following test for applications that seek to have statements of claims struck:

[19]      The
Supreme Court of Canada set out in
Odhavji Estate v. Woodhouse
,
2003 SCC 69 (CanLII)
, [2003] 3
S.C.R. 263 the test for striking out a statement of claim on the basis that it
disclosed no reasonable claim:

[14] ... a court
may strike out a statement of claim that discloses no reasonable cause of
action. The rules with respect to striking out a statement of claim are much
the same in other provinces. In British Columbia, for example, Rule 19(24)(a)
of the Rules of Court,
B.C. Reg. 221/90
, states that a court may strike out a
pleading on the ground that it discloses no reasonable claim.

[15] An
excellent statement of the test for striking out a claim under such provisions
is that set out by Wilson J. in
Hunt v. Carey Canada Inc.
,
1990 CanLII 90 (SCC)
, [1990] 2
S.C.R. 959, at p. 980:

... assuming
that the facts as stated in the statement of claim can be proved, is it
"plain and obvious" that the plaintiff's statement of claim discloses
no reasonable cause of action? As in England, if there is a chance that the
plaintiff might succeed, then the plaintiff should not be "driven from the
judgment seat". Neither the length and complexity of the issues, the
novelty of the cause of action, nor the potential for the defendant to present
a strong defence should prevent the plaintiff from proceeding with his or her
case. Only if the action is certain to fail because it contains a radical
defect ... should the relevant portions of a plaintiff's statement of claim be
struck out ... .

The test is a
stringent one. The facts are to be taken as pleaded. When so taken, the
question that must then be determined is whether ... it is "plain and
obvious" that the action must fail. It is only if the statement of claim
is certain to fail because it contains a "radical defect" that the
plaintiff should be driven from the judgment.

[16]      I agree with Ms. Neufeld’s
argument contained in her outline dated September 3, 2009. Dr. Nesbitt’s
statement of claim is prolix, and is little more than an irrelevant opinion of
Dr. Nesbitt and others, and events that have happened that have no relevance to
the claims being made. On this basis alone, it could be struck out in its
entirety (
Stephen v. British Columbia (Ministry of Children & Family
Development)
,
2008 BCSC 1656
).

[17]      There are conclusions of law plead
by Dr. Nesbitt that do not set out any of the material facts on which he
relies. In
Delaney & Friends Cartoon Productions Ltd
.,
2005 BCSC
371
, at para.
9
, Joyce J. states:

A material fact
is one that is essential in order to formulate a complete cause of action. If a
material fact is omitted, a cause of action is not effectively pleaded.

[18]      Dr. Nesbitt has failed to plead
the words or actions that he alleges are defamatory in accordance with Rule
19(12) of the Rules.

[19]      Scandalous, frivolous, vexatious
or embarrassing pleadings have been defined by Joyce J. in
Stephen
:

[50]      In
Citizens
for Foreign Aid Reform Inc. v. Canadian Jewish Congress
(1999),
1999 CanLII 5860 (BC SC)
, 36 C.P.C.
(4th) 266 (BCSC) at para.
47
, Romilly J. summarized what must be established in
order to find that pleadings are "unnecessary, scandalous, frivolous or
vexatious" under Rule 19(24)(b):

Irrelevancy and
embarrassment are both established when pleadings are so confusing that it is
difficult to understand what is being pleaded:
Gittings v. Caneco
Audio-Publishers Inc.
(1987),
1987 CanLII 2561 (BC SC)
, 17 B.C.L.R. (2d) 38 (BCSC). An
"embarrassing" and "scandalous" pleading is one that is so
irrelevant that it will involve the parties in useless expense and will
prejudice the trial of the action by involving them in a dispute apart from the
issues:
Keddie v. Dumas Hotels Ltd.
(1985),
1985 CanLII 417 (BC CA)
, 62 B.C.L.R. 145 (BCCA) at
147. An allegation which is scandalous will not be struck if it is relevant to
the proceedings. It will only be struck if irrelevant as well as scandalous:
College
of Dental Surgeons (British Columbia) v. Cleland
(1968),
1968 CanLII 1008 (BC CA)
, 66 W.W.R. 499
(BCCA). A pleading is "unnecessary" or "vexatious" if it
does not go to establishing the plaintiff's cause of action or does not advance
any claim known in law:
Strauts v. Harrigan
(December 2, 1991), Doc.
Vancouver C913631 (BCSC). A pleading that is superfluous will not be struck out
if it is not necessarily unnecessary or otherwise objectionable:
Lutz v.
Canadian Puget Sound Lumber

(1920), 28 B.C.R. 39 (BCCA)
. A pleading is
"frivolous" if it is obviously unsustainable, not in the sense that
it lacks an evidentiary basis, but because of the doctrine of estoppel:
Chrisgian
v. B.C. Rail Ltd.
(July 3, 1992) Doc. Prince George 20714 (B.C. Master).

[20]      Abuse of process is when a proceeding
is being used for some ulterior or improper purpose (
Budgell v. Oppal
,

2007 BCSC 991
).

[21]      I
will assess Dr. Nesbitt’s statement of claim in accordance with its headings
and paragraphs. I will not comment on each paragraph.

[
13
]

Applying those principles, I conclude that Dr.
Nesbitt’s amended statement of claim must also be struck. I will address each
paragraph by number and provide my conclusion.

1-2         There is no objection to these paragraphs; they merely
identify the parties.

3-4         These paragraphs reach conclusions of law without any
material facts.

5             This paragraph reaches a conclusion of law without any
material facts. Dr. Nesbitt also alleges that he has been maliciously
prosecuted. There is no cause of action in respect of malicious prosecution.

6             This paragraph addresses matters relevant to the
custody proceedings before the Provincial Court.

7             This paragraph is irrelevant.

8             Dr. Nesbitt’s recitation of his historical health
problems is irrelevant to his claim.

9             Whether or not Ms. Nesbitt was aware of Dr. Nesbitt’s
health problems is irrelevant to his claim.

10           This assertion is irrelevant to the plaintiff’s claim.

11-13     The relationship between the plaintiff and defendant which
resulted in the birth of their daughter is relevant to the custody matter, but
not to Dr. Nesbitt’s claim.

14           The relationship between the plaintiff and defendant
which resulted in the birth of their daughter is relevant to the custody
matter, but not to Dr. Nesbitt’s claim. Dr. Nesbitt has agreed that this
paragraph ought to be struck.

15        Dr. Nesbitt has agreed that this paragraph ought to be
struck.

16-18     These allegations may be relevant to the custody matter,
but not to Dr. Nesbitt’s claim.

19-34     These allegations relate to events occurring in 2005 and
2006. These matters are statute barred in accordance with
s. 3(2)
of the
Limitation
Act
, R.S.B.C. 1996, c. 266.

35-43     These allegations may relate to the custody matter before
the Provincial Court. They are irrelevant to Dr. Nesbitt’s claim.

44-67     Dr. Nesbitt has agreed that these paragraphs should be
struck because he has not provided any particulars. I have reviewed those
paragraphs and they also state conclusions of law. They may relate to the
custody matter before the Provincial Court.

68-163   The plaintiff has voluntarily struck these paragraphs.

[
14
]

Dr. Nesbitt’s amended statement of claim does
not disclose a reasonable claim or ones that can be resolved by amendments.
Some are barred by the
Limitation Act
and others are not properly plead.

[
15
]

This is the second opportunity Dr. Nesbitt has
had to file a statement of claim which conforms with the
Rules
. He has
not done so.

[
16
]

There is nothing to be gained by directing Dr.
Nesbitt to file an amended amended statement of claim. The basis of his claim
is without merit. It appears, as Hyslop J. found, that Dr. Nesbitt’s statement
of claim is intended to punish Ms. Neufeld.

Compliance with October 14, 2009 Order

[
17
]

The defendant also seeks an order that Dr.
Nesbitt is in breach of the October 14, 2009 order of Truscott J. and if
not, whether Dr. Nesbitt’s application for default judgment has merit.

[
18
]

I find that a decision on this issue is
unnecessary. It appears that Dr. Nesbitt did not abide by the order of
Truscott J. regarding the provision of unaltered exhibits. However, as I
have struck the statement of claim, the issue concerning whether
Dr. Nesbitt’s application for default judgment has merit is entirely
academic. He has no claim against Ms. Neufeld in these proceedings and
therefore he is not entitled default judgment.

Costs

[
19
]

Ms. Neufeld claims special costs which were
awarded to her by Hyslop J. and Crawford J. in the matters before
them.

[
20
]

Ms. Justice Crawford found, at para. 106:

Ms. Neufeld
sought special costs. I am of the opinion that she is clearly entitled. Relying
on
Garcia v. Crestbrook Forest Industries Ltd.
(1995),
1994 CanLII 2570 (BC CA)
, 9 B.C.L.R. (3d)
242, 45 B.C.A.C. 222, at para.
17
of B.C.L.R., and
Young v. Borzoni
,

2007 BCCA 16
, 277 D.L.R. (4th) 685, at para.
68
of BCCA, counsel for Ms.
Neufeld submitted that Dr. Nesbitt continued to subject Ms. Neufeld to the same
groundless claims in his pleadings; that his claims are designed to cause her
emotional suffering; and that they are malicious and relentless, deliberately
designed to humiliate Ms. Neufeld and force her to acknowledge him. I agree
that Dr. Nesbitt engaged in reprehensible conduct, giving rise to Ms. Neufeld's
counterclaim, and that his misconduct is deserving of the Court's reproof or
rebuke. Ms. Neufeld is entitled to special costs.

[
21
]

I reach the same conclusion in respect of the
matters before me. Ms. Neufeld is entitled to special costs.

Summary

[
22
]

Dr. Nesbitt’s statement of claim is struck.

[
23
]

Ms. Neufeld is entitled to special costs.

“Gropper
J.”
